source_text: Est in arcanis sanctarum litterarum transcendisse in Aegyptum cogente inopia rei frumentariae principem Hebraeorum cum omni domo et cognatione. cuius posteri cum diutius in Aegypto commorantes in magnam gentem creuissent et graui atque intolerando seruitutis iugo premerentur, percussit Aegyptum deus insanabili plaga et populum suum liberauit traductum medio mari, cum discissis fluctibus et in utramque partem dimotis per siccum populus graderetur. conatusque rex Aegyptiorum profugos insequi coeunte in statum suum pelago cum omnibus copiis interceptus est. quod facinus tam clarum tamque mirabile quamuis ad praesens uirtutem dei hominibus ostenderet, tamen praesignificatio et figura maioris rei fuit, quam deus idem in extrema temporum consummatione facturus est: liberabit enim plebem suam de graui seruitute mundi. sed quoniam tunc una plebs dei et aput unam gentem fuit, Aegyptus sola percussa est, nunc autem quia populus dei ex omnibus linguis congregatus aput omnes gentes commoratur et ab his dominantibus premitur, necesse est uniuersas nationes id est orbem totum caelestibus plagis uerberari, ut iustus et cultor dei populus liberetur. et sicut tunc signa facta sunt quibus futura clades Aegyptiis ostenderetur, ita in ultimo fient prodigia miranda per omnia elementa mundi, quibus imminens exitus uniuersis gentibus intellegatur. propinquante igitur huius saeculi termino humanarum rerum statum commutari necesse est et in deterius nequitia inualescente prolabi, ut iam nostra haec tempora, quibus iniquitas et malitia usque ad summum gradum creuit, in illius tamen insanabilis mali conparatione felicia et prope aurea possint iudicari. ita enim iustitia rarescet, ita inpietas et auaritia et cupiditas et libido crebrescet, ut si qui forte tum fuerint boni, praedae sint sceleratis ac diuexentur undique ab iniustis, soli autem mali opulenti sint, boni uero in omnibus contumeliis atque in egestate iactentur. confundetur omne ius et leges interibunt. nihil quisquam tunc habebit nisi aut quaesitum aut defensum manu, audacia et uis omnia possidebunt. non fides in hominibus, non pax, non humanitas, non pudor, non ueritas erit atque ita neque securitas neque regimen neque requies a malis ulla. omnis enim terra tumultuabitur, frement ubique bella, omnes gentes in armis erunt et se inuicem obpugnabunt: ciuitates inter se finitimae proeliabuntur et prima omnium Aegyptus stultarum superstitionum luet poenas et sanguine uelut flumine operietur. tum peragrabit gladius orbem metens omnia et tamquam messem cuncta prosternens. cuius uastitatis et confusionis haec erit causa, quod Romanum nomen, quo nunc regitur orbis — horret animus dicere, sed dicam, quia futurum est — tolletur e terra et inperium in Asiam reuertetur ac rursus oriens dominabitur atque occidens seruiet. nec mirum cuiquam debet uideri, si regnum tanta mole fundatum ac tamdiu per tot et tales uiros auctum, tantis denique opibus confirmatum aliquando tamen conruet. nihil est enim humanis uiribus laboratum quod non humanis aeque uiribus destrui possit, quoniam mortalia sunt opera mortalium. sic et alia prius regna cum diutius floruissent, nihilominus tamen occiderunt. nam et Aegyptios et Persas et Graecos et Assyrios proditum est regimen habuisse terrarum: quibus omnibus destructis ad Romanos quoque rerum summa peruenit. qui quanto ceteris omnibus regnis magnitudine antistant, tanto maiore decident lapsu, quia plus habent ponderis ad ruinam quae sunt ceteris altiora. non inscite Seneca Romanae urbis tempora distribuit in aetates. primam enim dixit infantiam sub rege Romulo fuisse, a quo et genita et quasi educata sit Roma; deinde pueritiam sub ceteris regibus, a quibus et aucta sit et disciplinis pluribus institutisque formata; at uero Tarquinio regnante cum iam quasi adulta esse coepisset, seruitium non tulisse et reiecto superbae dominationis iugo maluisse legibus obtemperare quam regibus; cumque esset adulescentia eius fine Punici belli terminata, tum denique confirmatis uiribus coepisse iuuenescere. sublata enim Carthagine, quae tam diu aemula imperii fuit, manus suas in totum orbem terra marique porrexit, donec regibus cunctis et nationibus imperio subiugatis cum iam bellorum materia deficeret, uiribus suis male uteretur, quibus se ipsa confecit. haec fuit prima eius senectus, cum bellis laeerata ciuilibus atque intestino malo pressa rursus ad regimen singularis imperii reccidit quasi ad alteram infantiam reuoluta. amissa enim libertate, quam Bruto duce et auctore defenderat, ita consenuit, tamquam sustentare se ipsa non ualeret, nisi adminiculo regentium niteretur. quodsi haec ita sunt, quid restat nisi ut sequatur interitus senectutem? et id futurum breui contiones prophetarum denuntiant sub ambage aliorum nominum, ne facile quis intellegat. Sibyllae tamen aperte interituram esse Romam locuntur et quidem iudicio dei, quod nomen eius habuerit inuisum et inimica iustitiae alumnum ueritatis populum trucidarit. Hystaspes quoque, qui fuit Medorum rex antiquissimus, a quo amnis nomen accepit qui nunc Hydaspes dicitur, admirabile somnium sub interpretatione uaticinantis pueri ad memoriam posteris tradidit: sublatuiri ex orbe imperium nomenque Romanum multo ante praefatus est quam illa Troiana gens conderetur.
pass_a_gloss: There is in the secrets of the holy writings that the leader of the Hebrews with his whole house and family was compelled by the lack of grain to cross over into Egypt. Whose descendants, having dwelled in Egypt for a longer time, had grown into a great nation and were being pressed by the heavy and intolerable yoke of servitude, God struck Egypt with an incurable plague and liberated his people, who had been led through the middle of the sea, when the waves were torn apart and the people walked on dry land with the waves pushed aside on both sides. And the king of the Egyptians, having attempted to pursue the fugitives, was intercepted with all his forces when the sea came together again. This deed, as glorious and as wondrous as it was, although it showed the power of God to men at that time, was nevertheless a foreshadowing and a figure of a greater thing that the same God will do at the end of times: for he will liberate his people from the heavy servitude of the world. But since at that time there was only one people of God and it was among one nation, only Egypt was struck; now, however, since the people of God, gathered from all languages, dwell among all nations and are being oppressed by those who dominate them, it is necessary that all nations, that is, the whole world, be scourged by heavenly plagues, so that the just and God-fearing people may be liberated. And just as signs were then made by which the future destruction of the Egyptians was shown, so in the last times wonderful prodigies will occur through all the elements of the world, by which the imminent end of all nations will be understood. Therefore, as the end of this age approaches, it is necessary that the state of human affairs be changed and decline for the worse, as wickedness grows stronger, so that our times, in which iniquity and malice have grown to the highest degree, may be judged fortunate and almost golden in comparison to that incurable evil. For justice will be so scarce, and impiety and greed and lust will be so frequent, that if there happen to be any good people, they will be prey to the wicked and will be driven away on all sides by the unjust, and only the wicked will be wealthy, while the good will be cast away in all kinds of contempt and poverty. All law will be confounded, and laws will perish. No one will have anything then except what they have acquired or defended by hand, and audacity and force will possess everything. There will be no faith in men, no peace, no humanity, no shame, no truth, and therefore no security, no rule, no rest from evils. For the whole earth will be in turmoil, with wars raging everywhere, and all nations will be in arms and will attack each other: neighboring cities will fight each other, and first of all, Egypt will pay the penalty for its foolish superstitions and will be covered in blood like a river. Then the sword will traverse the world, cutting down everything, and laying low all things like a harvest. The cause of this devastation and confusion will be that the Roman name, by which the world is now ruled - my soul shudders to say it, but I will say it, because it will happen - will be removed from the earth, and the empire will return to Asia, and the East will dominate again, and the West will serve. Nor should it seem wonderful to anyone if a kingdom, founded with such great strength and increased for so long by so many and such great men, and finally confirmed by such great resources, should nonetheless collapse at some point. For there is nothing that has been built up by human strength that cannot be destroyed by human strength, since the works of mortals are mortal. Thus also other kingdoms, which had flourished for a longer time, have nonetheless perished. For the Egyptians and the Persians and the Greeks and the Assyrians have been said to have had dominion over the earth: and when all these were destroyed, the sum of things came to the Romans. Who, the more they excel all other kingdoms in greatness, will fall with a greater collapse, because they have more weight to bring about their ruin, which is higher than that of others. Seneca did not foolishly divide the times of the Roman city into ages. For he said that the first age was infancy under King Romulus, from whom Rome was born and, as it were, educated; then childhood under the other kings, by whom it was increased and formed by many disciplines and institutions; but when Tarquinius was reigning, since Rome had already begun to be, as it were, an adult, it did not tolerate servitude and, having rejected the yoke of proud domination, preferred to obey laws rather than kings; and when its adolescence was ended with the finish of the Punic War, it finally began to grow strong, its forces having been confirmed. For when Carthage, which had been a rival of the empire for so long, was destroyed, it stretched out its hands over the whole world, by land and sea, until, with all kings and nations having been subjugated by its empire, and when the material for wars was already lacking, it began to use its forces badly, by which it destroyed itself. This was its first old age, when, worn out by civil wars and pressed by internal evil, it fell back into the rule of a single empire, as if it had been turned back to a second infancy. For having lost the liberty which it had defended under the leadership and authority of Brutus, it grew old, as if it were not able to sustain itself, unless it were supported by the aid of rulers. But if these things are so, what remains except that destruction follows old age? And this will happen soon, as the prophecies of the prophets announce under the ambiguity of other names, so that no one may easily understand. The Sibyls, however, say openly that Rome will perish, and indeed by the judgment of God, because it has had a name that is hated and has killed the people of truth, the foster child of justice. Hystaspes also, who was the most ancient king of the Medes, from whom the river that is now called the Hydaspes received its name, handed down to the memory of posterity an admirable dream under the interpretation of a prophesying boy: he had said long before that the empire and the name of the Romans would be removed from the world, before the Trojan nation was founded.
pass_b_english: In the hidden depths of the holy writings we read that the leader of the Hebrews, together with his whole household and kin, was forced by a shortage of grain to cross into Egypt (Exodus 1:14). His descendants, after dwelling there for a long time, grew into a great nation and were crushed beneath a heavy, intolerable yoke of slavery; God struck Egypt with an incurable plague and delivered his people, leading them through the midst of the sea while the waves were split apart and driven to either side so that the people walked on dry ground (Exodus 14:13-31). When the Egyptian king tried to pursue the fugitives, the sea returned to its place and engulfed him with all his forces.

That deed, glorious and wondrous as it was, displayed God's power to humanity at that moment, yet it served only as a foreshadowing and a figure of a greater act that the same God will perform at the consummation of the ages: he will free his people from the heavy servitude of the world. In those days there was but one people of God, confined to a single nation, so only Egypt was struck; now, however, the people of God, gathered from every tongue, dwell among all nations and are oppressed by their rulers, and therefore it is necessary that all nations — that is, the whole world — be scourged by heavenly plagues so that the just and God‑fearing people may be liberated. Just as signs were given then to reveal the coming destruction of the Egyptians, so in the last days marvelous portents will appear through every element of the world, by which the imminent end of all nations will be recognized.

As the end of this age draws near, the condition of human affairs must change and deteriorate, because wickedness grows stronger, so that our present times — in which iniquity and malice have reached their highest pitch — may be judged fortunate and almost golden by comparison with that incurable evil. Justice will become so rare, and impiety, greed, and lust so rampant, that any good people who happen to exist will become prey for the wicked and will be driven away on every side by the unjust; only the wicked will be wealthy, while the good will be cast into every kind of contempt and poverty. All law will be confounded and statutes will perish; no one will possess anything except what they have seized or defended by hand, and audacity and force will rule everything. There will be no faith among men, no peace, no humanity, no shame, no truth, and consequently no security, no government, no rest from evils. The whole earth will be in turmoil, wars will rage everywhere, all nations will be armed and will attack one another; neighboring cities will fight each other, and first of all Egypt will pay the penalty for its foolish superstitions, drenched in blood as if by a river.

Then the sword will sweep across the world, cutting down everything and laying all things low like a harvest. The cause of this devastation and confusion will be that the Roman name, by which the world is now governed — my soul shudders to speak it, but I must, because it will happen — will be removed from the earth, the empire will revert to Asia, the East will dominate once more, and the West will serve. No one should be surprised if a kingdom founded with such immense strength, enlarged for so long by so many and such great men, and finally secured by such vast resources, should nevertheless collapse at some point. For nothing built by human power cannot be undone by human power, since the works of mortals are mortal. Thus other kingdoms that flourished for a long time have nonetheless perished: the Egyptians, Persians, Greeks, and Assyrians are recorded to have held dominion over the earth, and when they were all destroyed, supreme authority passed to the Romans. The more the Romans surpass all other kingdoms in greatness, the greater will be their fall, because the higher they rise, the more weight they carry toward ruin.

Seneca did not foolishly divide the history of the Roman city into ages. He said the first age was infancy under King Romulus, from whom Rome was born and, as it were, nurtured; then childhood under the subsequent kings, by whom it was enlarged and shaped by many disciplines and institutions; but when Tarquinius reigned, Rome had already begun to be, as it were, an adult, and it could not endure servitude, so it rejected the yoke of proud domination and chose to obey laws rather than kings. When its adolescence ended with the conclusion of the Punic War, it finally began to mature, its strength confirmed. After Carthage, the long‑standing rival of the empire, was destroyed, Rome stretched its hands over the whole world by land and sea until every king and nation had been subdued; then, with no more wars to fight, it misused its own power and destroyed itself. This was its first old age, when, worn out by civil wars and pressed by internal corruption, it fell back under the rule of a single emperor, as if returning to a second infancy. Having lost the liberty it had defended under Brutus's leadership and authority, it aged as though unable to sustain itself without the support of rulers. If these things are so, what remains but that destruction follows old age? And this will happen soon, as the prophecies of the prophets announce under the veil of other names so that no one may easily understand. The Sibyls, however, declare openly that Rome will perish, and indeed by the judgment of God, because it bore a name hated by God and slaughtered the people of truth, the foster child of justice. Hystaspes, the most ancient king of the Medes, from whom the river now called the Hydaspes takes its name, transmitted to posterity an admirable dream through the interpretation of a prophesying boy: he foretold long before the founding of the Trojan nation that the empire and the Roman name would be removed from the world.
notes: The Latin text is from Lactantius' Divine Institutes 7.15

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful gloss, and Pass B provides a polished English version that includes necessary scripture citations (Exodus 1:14, Exodus 14:13-31) which were alluded to in the Latin. All clauses, including the complex historical/prophetic sections regarding Rome and Seneca, are preserved in sense and agency.
